paras: The lynching of an unnamed gambler near Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, took place in mid-December 1888, when a mob took a Black man from the posse that had arrested him and hanged him from a tree. He was accused of leading an armed party that fired on a railroad contractor's camp after laborers had driven him away. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country, and later weekly digests misreported it as the lynching of a man who had fatally wounded a "Captain Dunnavant" near Chattanooga.

The setting was the line of a new railroad being built to Cumberland Gap, where Capt. S. D. Dunavint, described as "a prominent contractor," had a camp of laborers. According to a special to the Nashville American from Knoxville, "an unknown negro gambler" was driven from the works by the laborers.

The man returned shortly with about a dozen men, called "desperadoes," all armed with Winchester rifles. They fired several shots at Dunavint, "none of which took effect," and the party was dispersed; a shorter Knoxville dispatch said they were driven off "without any injuries having been inflicted." That dispatch, dated December 18, placed the attack on the camp "yesterday."

A posse arrested the leader at Cumberland Gap and started toward Tazewell with him. On the way the posse was surrounded by a mob, numbered at 100 in the Savannah and Richmond copies, "over a hundred" in a Knoxville version, and 200 in the Rock Island Argus. The mob took the prisoner from the officers and "swung him to the nearest tree."
The coverage does not name the dead man or report an inquest, arrests of mob members, or any official response.

Two separately worded versions circulated on December 19. A brief Knoxville item ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under the headline "Made Short Work of Him" and in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, where it followed reports of armed clashes between Black and white men at Wahalak, Mississippi, and near Jackson, Tennessee. The Los Angeles Daily Herald compressed the same item into a paragraph of "Eastern Echoes."

The longer Nashville American special appeared in the Savannah Morning News as "Two Tragedies. One a Lynching, and the Other Fratricide by Stabbing" and in the Richmond Dispatch, both pairing it with the stabbing death of a Black man by his half brother near the same place. The Rock Island Argus printed it twice under "A Negro Gambler's Fate. Taken from the Officers by a Mob and Lynched," and the Evening Journal and Waterbury Evening Democrat ran it as "Two Tennessee Tragedies." None of these papers commented on the lynching, and none questioned the account of the attack on the camp.

A week later a one-sentence digest item ran in Minnesota, Dakota and North Dakota weeklies, including the Mower County Transcript, the Worthington Advance, the Hand County Press, the Kanabec County Times and the Griggs Courier. It stated that "a negro who shot and fatally wounded Captain Dunnavant" near Chattanooga on the 18th "was caught and lynched."

The reports disagree on whether Dunavant was hurt: both wire versions say the shots missed, while the later digest says he was fatally wounded. The digest also places the event near Chattanooga rather than on the Cumberland Gap line, and the wire reports, datelined Knoxville and closer to the event, are the more detailed evidence. Copies of the Nashville special give Dunavant's initials as "S. D." or "G. D." and the mob as 100 or 200.

accounts.label: Short Knoxville wire
accounts.gist: The gambler and friends tried to shoot some of the men, were driven off with no injuries, and the leader was arrested; on the road to jail a mob took him from the officers and hanged him.

accounts.label: Nashville American special from Knoxville
accounts.gist: A dozen men with Winchesters fired at Capt. S. D. Dunavint without effect; a posse arrested the leader at Cumberland Gap and, heading for Tazewell, was surrounded by a mob of 100 (or 200) who hanged him.

accounts.label: Weekly news digest
accounts.gist: A man who 'shot and fatally wounded Captain Dunnavant' on the 18th near Chattanooga was caught and lynched.

framing.detail: Brief wire items with no comment; headlines 'Made Short Work of Him' (A1) and 'A Negro Gambler's Fate. Taken from the Officers by a Mob and Lynched' (A9) present the lynching as a deserved end.
The Savannah Morning News and Richmond Dispatch paired it with a stabbing as 'Two Tragedies' (A7, A4).

conflicts.note: The digest is later, compressed and far from the scene; the two independent wire versions agree no one was hit.
